items.followUp: Why is aluminium commonly used for making overhead electrical cables?

rubric.why: Copper’s high electrical conductivity allows electric current to pass through easily.
rubric.description: States that copper is a good conductor of electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking copper’s use in wires to its high electrical conductivity.

rubric.why: Ductility allows copper to be drawn into thin wires.
rubric.description: States that copper is ductile or can be drawn into wires.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying copper’s ductility or its ability to be made into wires.

modelAnswer: Copper is a good conductor of electricity, so current passes through it easily.
Copper is ductile and can be drawn into thin wires.

items.followUp: Why is sodium more electropositive than lithium?

rubric.why: Calcium is below magnesium in Group 2 and has a larger atomic radius.
rubric.description: States that calcium has a larger atomic size or radius than magnesium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the increase in atomic size down the group.

rubric.why: Calcium’s outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and are lost more readily, making calcium more electropositive.
rubric.description: Explains that calcium loses its outer electrons more readily because the nuclear attraction is weaker.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking weaker attraction or easier electron loss to greater electropositivity.

modelAnswer: Calcium is below magnesium in Group 2 and has a larger atomic size.
Its outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and experience weaker attraction, so calcium loses them more readily and is more electropositive.

items.followUp: Why is pure silver not generally used to make durable jewellery?

rubric.why: Pure gold is too soft for ornaments that need to retain their shape.
rubric.description: States that pure gold is soft.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the softness of pure gold.

rubric.why: Gold is alloyed with other metals to increase its hardness and durability.
rubric.description: States that gold is mixed with other metals to make it harder or more durable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the use of a gold alloy.

modelAnswer: No, pure gold is too soft to make durable ornaments.
It is mixed with other metals to form a harder alloy that is more suitable for making ornaments.

items.followUp: Write any five properties of canal rays.

rubric.why: Cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles, which are electrons.
rubric.description: Identifies cathode rays as negatively charged particles or electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating their negative charge or electron nature.

rubric.why: Cathode rays travel in straight lines in the absence of an electric or magnetic field.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Their negative charge causes them to be deflected towards the positive plate in an electric field.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays are deflected towards the positive plate by an electric field.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the direction or electric-field deflection.

rubric.why: Cathode rays are deflected by a magnetic field, showing that they are charged particles in motion.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays are deflected by a magnetic field.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Cathode rays show properties such as producing fluorescence, casting shadows, or having the same nature regardless of the gas or electrode material.
rubric.description: Gives another valid property of cathode rays, such as producing fluorescence, casting shadows, or being independent of the gas and electrode material.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid additional property.

modelAnswer: Cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles called electrons.
They travel in straight lines.
They are deflected towards the positive plate in an electric field.
They are deflected by a magnetic field.
Their properties are independent of the gas in the discharge tube and the material of the electrodes.

items.followUp: Write notes on any four branches of chemistry other than those described in this question.

rubric.why: Physical chemistry studies the physical properties of matter and the energy changes accompanying chemical reactions.
rubric.description: Correctly describes physical chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the branch and giving its subject of study.

rubric.why: Organic chemistry deals mainly with carbon compounds, including hydrocarbons and their derivatives.
rubric.description: Correctly describes organic chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the branch and giving its subject of study.

rubric.why: Inorganic chemistry studies elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
rubric.description: Correctly describes inorganic chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the branch and giving its subject of study.

rubric.why: Biochemistry applies chemistry to substances and processes in living organisms.
rubric.description: Correctly describes biochemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the branch and giving its subject of study.

modelAnswer: Physical chemistry studies the physical properties of matter and the energy changes involved in chemical reactions.
Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, especially hydrocarbons and their derivatives.
Inorganic chemistry studies elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
Biochemistry studies the substances and chemical processes of living organisms.

items.followUp: Define intermolecular forces and explain how they affect boiling point and viscosity.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction involving hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom and another electronegative atom with a lone pair.
rubric.description: Defines hydrogen bonding and identifies the atoms or intermolecular attraction involved.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as an intermolecular attraction and 1 mark for describing the hydrogen–electronegative atom interaction.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding requires extra energy to overcome, raising boiling points.
rubric.description: States that hydrogen bonding raises boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this effect.

rubric.why: Stronger attractions between molecules can also raise melting point.
rubric.description: States that hydrogen bonding raises melting point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this effect.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding can increase viscosity and surface tension, and can improve the solubility of polar substances in water.
rubric.description: Gives another valid physical-property effect of hydrogen bonding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid effect such as increased viscosity, surface tension, or water solubility.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom, such as F, O or N, and a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
Hydrogen bonding strengthens the attraction between molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them.
It generally raises the boiling point of a substance.
It can also raise melting point and increase viscosity or surface tension.
Hydrogen bonding can make polar molecules more soluble in water.

items.followUp: Define melting point and discuss the effects of pressure, intermolecular forces and impurities on it.

rubric.why: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure.
rubric.description: Defines boiling point using vapour pressure and external pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: Greater external pressure requires a higher temperature for vapour pressure to match it; reduced pressure lowers the boiling point.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of external pressure on boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct pressure relationship.

rubric.why: Stronger attractions between molecules require more energy to overcome, increasing boiling point.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of intermolecular forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking stronger intermolecular forces to a higher boiling point.

rubric.why: A non-volatile impurity generally raises a liquid’s boiling point.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of a non-volatile impurity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that non-volatile impurities raise boiling point.

modelAnswer: The boiling point is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid becomes equal to the external pressure.
Increasing external pressure raises the boiling point, while decreasing pressure lowers it.
Stronger intermolecular forces raise the boiling point because more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
A non-volatile impurity generally raises the boiling point of a liquid.

items.followUp: Explain how pressure affects the solubility of gases in liquids.

rubric.why: The solubility of most solid solutes in water increases as temperature rises.
rubric.description: States the usual effect of increasing temperature on the solubility of solids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the general increase in solubility of most solids.

rubric.why: Heating favours dissolution when the process absorbs heat.
rubric.description: Explains the increase for an endothermic dissolution process.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking heat absorption or endothermic dissolution to increased solubility.

rubric.why: Gas solubility in liquids generally decreases as temperature rises.
rubric.description: States the general effect of increasing temperature on gas solubility.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the decrease in gas solubility.

rubric.why: Heating gives dissolved gas particles more energy to escape from the liquid; gas dissolution is generally exothermic.
rubric.description: Explains why warming decreases gas solubility.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that heating promotes escape of gas or linking the effect to exothermic dissolution.

modelAnswer: The solubility of most solid solutes in water increases as temperature increases.
For an endothermic dissolution, added heat favours dissolving and increases solubility; for some substances with exothermic dissolution, solubility may decrease as temperature rises.
The solubility of gases in liquids generally decreases as temperature increases.
Heating gives dissolved gas particles more energy to escape from the liquid.
